h1: Talus hops for pink grapefruit and rose in modern IPAs
title: Talus Hops for Pink Grapefruit and Rose | Craft Beer School
desc: Talus hops explained for homebrewers: pink grapefruit, rose and tangerine aroma, a 20 litre IPA recipe with hop weights and how to dry hop it well.
teaser: Talus smells of pink grapefruit and rose petals. It is an unusual pair that makes a pale IPA easy to tell apart.
standfirst: Talus is a modern American aroma hop with a pink grapefruit and floral rose character. It suits a clean, fairly dry IPA. Here is a 20 litre recipe, the hop weights and the mistakes that flatten it.
sections: A hop with a floral side

Most American citrus hops lean on pith and pine. Talus is different. Drinkers and brewers describe pink grapefruit, tangerine and a rose-like floral note, with a light resinous backbone underneath. We treat it as a hop to build a beer around rather than a hop to bury in a blend.

The floral note comes from terpene alcohols in the hop oil, mainly geraniol and linalool. They are water soluble enough to survive into the finished beer, which is why rosy and perfumed notes often show up more in a dry hopped ale than in one hopped only in the kettle. Alpha acid is moderate, high enough to make Talus useful in the boil as well. Read the figure on your own pack rather than a table, because it moves with the crop.

Rose and pink grapefruit are delicate next to caramel or toffee. A sweet, heavy base turns them to marmalade. Keep the grist simple and the finish dry.

For 20 litres at about OG 1.056, use 4.0 kg pale malt (80%), 0.5 kg wheat malt (10%) and 0.5 kg flaked oats (10%). Mash at 66 °C for 60 minutes. The oats and wheat give a soft mouthfeel without sweetness. Ferment with a clean American ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. A finishing gravity near 1.012 gives about 5.8% ABV from (1.056 - 1.012) x 131.25.
A hop schedule that shows it off

Here is a working schedule for the same 20 litres, aiming for about 28 IBU. That is moderate on purpose, so the hop aroma does the talking.

  • 10 g of a clean 14% alpha bittering hop at 60 minutes, for roughly 17 IBU.
  • 40 g Talus in a 20 minute whirlpool at 80 °C, adding about 10 IBU.
  • 80 g Talus dry hop (4 g per litre), at the end of active fermentation.

Those IBU figures are estimates. Whirlpool utilisation depends on temperature, time and hop form, so treat 28 as a target to taste against, not a measurement.
The floor detail: dry hop timing and contact

The rose note is the first thing to go wrong. Leave a heavy dry hop on the beer for a week at 20 °C and the floral top note turns to grass and tea. We prefer a dry hop of about three days, then a cold crash and a quick rack off the hops.

Oxygen is the second enemy. Pick-up during a dry hop addition or transfer browns the beer and flattens aroma within weeks. Purge the fermenter with CO2 before you open it, add the hops quickly and close it again. Our guide to Strata covers a hop that behaves differently under the same treatment, which is a useful contrast.

Talus pairs well with hops that add a different fruit rather than more of the same. A small share of a tropical hop gives a pink grapefruit and mango mix. Pine hops such as Columbus push it towards a dank, resinous IPA and bury the rose.

If you are new to the hop, brew it alone first. A single hop beer is the cheapest way to learn what a variety does. Taste it again at two and four weeks, because hop character changes in the package.
Buying and storing it in India

Talus is not always on Indian homebrew supplier lists. When it is, the pack may have crossed a warm port. Ask for the harvest year. Buy sealed foil packs, keep them frozen and open only what you need for a brew. Terpene alcohols are more stable than the lighter hop oils, but alpha acids and fresh aroma still fade with warmth and air.

If you cannot get it, a split of Citra and a floral hop such as Hallertau Blanc is a rough stand-in, though it will not match.
A split test to learn the hop

Brew the 20 litre batch to the end of the boil with only the bittering hop and the whirlpool charge. Split the wort into two 10 litre fermenters. Dry hop one with 40 g of Talus and the other with 40 g of a pine-led hop you know well. Same yeast, same temperature, same day.

Package both and taste them side by side at two weeks. The contrast teaches more than any description. It also shows where hop aroma comes from. Yeast contact, oxygen control and dry hop chemistry decide whether it survives. That is the territory where structured science starts to pay off.
faqs: What does Talus hop taste like?
Pink grapefruit, tangerine and a rose-like floral note, with some light resin. It is more perfumed than a typical pine and pith American hop.
Can Talus be used for bittering?
Yes, because its alpha acid is moderate. Most brewers still keep it for the whirlpool and dry hop to get the most from the aroma.
How much Talus should I dry hop with?
About 3 to 5 g per litre for a pale IPA, with three days of contact. Longer contact at warm temperatures can turn the floral note grassy.
